query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored sub-solvus aging treatment that induces a uniform dispersion of coherent nanoscale precipitates in the refractory HEA matrix will enhance the alloy’s high-temperature strength and creep resistance while preserving its low density and room‐temperature ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy with a body-centered cubic matrix that exhibits acceptable room-temperature mechanical properties but insufficient high-temperature performance (e.g., creep resistance) without the density penalty incurred by heavy element additions.
generation.intervention: Apply a sub-solvus aging treatment by annealing the alloy at a temperature slightly below the solvus limit for precipitate formation and holding for an optimized time to induce a uniform and nanoscale precipitate distribution.
generation.conditions: Aging treatment conditions determined from the alloy’s phase diagram (temperature below the solvus, precise time duration); subsequent evaluation under high-temperature conditions (around 1000–1200°C) under sustained or cyclic mechanical loads, with parallel room-temperature tensile tests to confirm that ductility and strength are maintained.
generation.structural_mediator: A uniform distribution of finely dispersed, coherent nanoscale precipitates (such as an L1_2 or similar phase) within the primary BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The coherent precipitates serve as effective obstacles to dislocation motion during high-temperature loading, thereby improving strength retention and creep resistance. Since the overall alloy composition is not altered, and the precipitates are nanoscale and coherent, the room-temperature ductility and the low density of the alloy remain largely unaffected.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast or solutionized baseline, the aged alloy will exhibit significantly higher high-temperature yield strength and reduced creep rates at 1000–1200°C, while maintaining similar room-temperature tensile strength and ductility, with no appreciable increase in density.
generation.baseline: The untreated or traditionally processed refractory HEA that lacks a controlled nanoscale precipitate distribution, resulting in insufficient high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected primarily under high-temperature mechanical loading conditions; if the aging treatment parameters deviate too far from the optimized sub-solvus range, there may be either insufficient precipitate formation or coarsening that could compromise the beneficial effects.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal aging temperature and duration need further optimization and may vary with specific alloy compositions and processing histories. Moreover, the exact precipitate chemistry and its evolution during extended exposure to high temperatures remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens from the same refractory HEA. Subject one set to the optimized sub-solvus aging treatment while keeping the other set as the untreated baseline. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to confirm the presence and distribution of nanoscale precipitates in the treated specimens. Perform high-temperature mechanical tests (creep and tensile tests at 1000–1200°C) and room-temperature tensile tests on both sets.
measurements: Creep rate under a constant load at 1000–1200°C
Microstructural characterization (precipitate size and distribution via TEM/SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in high-temperature strength and creep resistance compared to the untreated baseline, or if there is a measurable degradation in room-temperature ductility or strength, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . decision.trend: Earlier works on refractory high-entropy alloys have attempted to boost high‐temperature strength either by alloying with additional refractory elements or by using processing methods that foster in‐situ formation of reinforcement phases (e.g., ceramic particles in PMC7513042) or grain refinement via advanced melting and rapid solidification techniques (as in PMC11206460). Although these approaches do achieve improvements in high-temperature mechanical behavior such as increased compressive strength or creep resistance, they often do so at the cost of added density or compromised room-temperature ductility. There has been interest in thermal or thermomechanical treatments that modify the microstructure (for example, by precipitate formation) without a compositional change, but a single, controllable intervention that provides both high-temperature performance and preservation of room temperature properties remains elusive.
decision.unsolved: A method that meaningfully improves high-temperature strength and creep resistance in refractory HEAs, while avoiding the density penalty of heavy-element alloying and not sacrificing room-temperature ductility, is still needed.
decision.lever: Implement a sub-solvus aging treatment tailored to induce a uniform distribution of coherent, nanoscale precipitates within the matrix
decision.why: This next step follows the observed trend that controlled thermal processing can yield microscale architectural changes that impair high-temperature dislocation motion without modifying the alloy's overall composition. By optimizing the aging temperature and time (e.g., targeting conditions below the solvus to promote fine, coherent precipitate formation), one expects to reinforce the matrix during high-temperature service (around 1000–1200°C under sustained or cyclic loads) while leaving the room-temperature ductility and low-density benefits intact. Such a treatment lever builds directly on insights from previous studies and addresses the remaining gap.
